questions.stem: Identify the three questions to ask about any table before reading it.
options: Who is in it and who is missing? When was it collected? How was it measured, and by whom?
Is it big? Is it colourful? Is it recent?
Who made it? How much did it cost? Is it approved?
questions.why: Professionals interrogate the table first. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Describe survivor bias.
options: Analysing the customers, staff or products still here and concluding something about the ones that left
questions.why: The most expensive error in business data. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Explain why a satisfaction survey can mislead.
options: It contains the customers who stayed; the ones who left are not in the room
questions.why: Who is missing matters. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Identify the fourth question to ask of a table.
options: What would have to be in this table for me to be WRONG — and is it here?
questions.why: The fourth question tests your own conclusion. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Explain why 'when was it collected?' matters.
options: Data from before a competitor opened describes a different world
questions.why: What has changed since? See §5.1.

questions.stem: Describe when an average misleads.
options: When a few very large or small values pull it
questions.why: An average is honest when values cluster. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Describe the median.
options: The middle value when sorted — the safer default
questions.why: Rarely misleads. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Identify the rule of thumb for reporting the middle of a set of numbers.
options: Quote the median and the range together
questions.why: Two numbers, almost impossible to mislead with. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Identify the average and the median of 20, 20, 25, 25, 30, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50 and 735.
questions.why: One value of 735 pulls the average. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Explain what the range hides.
options: How the values are spread between the lowest and highest
questions.why: Range never misleads but hides the spread. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Describe what a percentage hides.
options: What it is a percentage OF
questions.why: Find what it is a percentage of before you react. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Identify the question to ask when told 'sales rose 200%'.
questions.why: From 2 units to 6. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Identify the habit the chapter says to build with percentages.
options: Always write the raw number beside the percentage — '30% (3 of 10)'
questions.why: '30%' alone is a claim you have not checked. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Explain why 'costs fell 15%' may not be good news.
options: Revenue may have fallen 22% in the same period
questions.why: 'Compared with what else?' See §5.3.

questions.stem: Describe the result of a 5% rise followed by a 5% fall.
options: You are below where you started
You are back where you started
You are above where you started
questions.why: Percentage of which base? See §5.3.

questions.stem: Identify the four ways a chart misleads while every number is true.
options: Cut axis, chosen window, two scales, missing base
Wrong colours, small font, 3D bars, no title
Fake numbers, fake dates, fake labels, fake source
Too many lines, too few lines, no lines, dotted lines
questions.why: All four are easy to spot once named. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Describe the cut-axis trick.
options: Starting the scale at 90 instead of 0, so tiny gaps look huge
questions.why: Where does the vertical axis begin? See §5.4.

questions.stem: Describe the chosen-window trick.
options: Showing only the months that support the story
questions.why: What happened before and after? See §5.4.

questions.stem: Describe the missing-base trick.
options: Showing counts where the populations differ wildly — per what?
questions.why: Per branch, per customer, per hour? See §5.4.

questions.stem: Identify the professional response to a misleading chart.
options: Ask 'could I see it with the axis from zero, and the full period?'
questions.why: You will get a better chart or a useful silence. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Identify the three explanations for two things rising together other than one causing the other.
options: It runs the other way; a third thing causes both; coincidence
questions.why: Each is common in business. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Describe 'it runs the other way'.
options: You assume advertising raised sales, but rising sales may have released the advertising budget
questions.why: Reverse causation. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Describe what raises a correlation toward a cause.
options: A mechanism you can explain, a sequence in the right order, and the IS NOT test
questions.why: Mechanism, sequence, IS NOT. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Explain what two points on a line prove.
options: A correlation strong enough to act on
questions.why: With enough measures some pairs move together by chance. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Identify what the course expects you to say about causation.
options: Honestly which of the four you are holding — cause, reverse, third thing or coincidence
questions.why: You are not expected to prove causation. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Identify the four steps for deciding what evidence would settle a question.
options: The question, the evidence, the threshold, the source
questions.why: Decide before you collect. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Explain why step 3, the threshold, matters most.
options: Without a threshold agreed in advance, any result can be read as supporting what you already believed
It is the hardest to write
It is required by the client
questions.why: Confirmation bias with a spreadsheet. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Describe the question in step 1.
options: One sentence, answerable yes or no — 'are regulars visiting less often than last year?'
questions.why: One sentence, yes or no. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Explain why professionals decide what would settle the question before collecting data.
options: Because that decides what to gather
Because it is faster to collect
questions.why: Students collect first and ask later. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Describe the source in step 4.
options: Where the evidence exists and who can give it — 'loyalty database; the marketing manager'
questions.why: Step 4 names where and who. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Explain why the spread is 'the actual problem'.
options: Not knowing how tightly values sit around the middle is what makes an average mislead
questions.why: Not knowing the spread is the problem. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Describe the two-scales trick.
options: Two lines on different scales so they appear to move together
questions.why: Are both lines on the same axis? See §5.4.

questions.stem: Analyse the gym survey: branch B scores 3.9 from 38 replies. Determine who is missing.
questions.why: The survey contains the customers who stayed. See §5.1 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Determine why 'who is missing' matters most for a gym.
options: Drop-outs are the gym's main problem, and they are exactly who did not answer
questions.why: Who is not in the room. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Select the data not in the gym table that could change the conclusion about branch B.
options: Cancellation rates by branch, from the membership system
questions.why: Something that tests the conclusion, from a real source. See Exercise 1 and §5.1.

questions.stem: Classify 'complaints' when it means written complaints only.
options: A measurement definition someone chose — ask how it was measured
questions.why: How was it measured, and by whom? See §5.1.

questions.stem: Analyse twelve tables spending 90–180 dirhams plus one corporate table of 1,495. Determine the number that describes a normal evening.
options: The median (about 125) — the 1,495 pulls the average
questions.why: Median and range together. See §5.2 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine what the restaurant manager is claiming credit for with 'average spend 240, up 12%'.
options: One corporate booking of eighteen people, not his pricing strategy
questions.why: Recalculate without the corporate table. See Exercise 2 and §5.2.

questions.stem: Select the honest sentence for the restaurant report.
options: 'Typical table spend was 90–180 dirhams (median about 125); one corporate booking of 1,495 raised the average to 240'
questions.why: Median, range and raw numbers. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager planning staff levels on the average of 96 when the median is 30. Determine the risk.
options: Plans for a customer who almost never appears
questions.why: Plan with the median when one value pulls the average. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Analyse '30% of customers complained'. Determine the question to ask first.
options: 'How many people is that?' — it may be 3 of 10 replies
questions.why: 30% of the ten who replied. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Classify a report line that reads '45%' with no raw number.
options: A claim you have not checked
questions.why: Percentages without raw numbers lose marks. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Analyse 'costs fell 15% — a success' when revenue fell 22%. Determine the honest reading.
options: Costs fell less than revenue, so the position got worse
questions.why: Compared with what else? See §5.3.

questions.stem: Determine the price after a 5% rise then a 5% fall on 100.
questions.why: Percentage of which base? See §5.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a chart with the vertical axis from 88% to 94%. Determine the trick and its effect.
options: Cut axis — a tiny gap looks enormous
questions.why: Where does the axis begin? See §5.4 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Analyse a supplier chart showing only April to September. Determine the trick.
options: Chosen window — what happened before and after?
questions.why: Shows the months that support the story. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Analyse complaints plotted on a separate right-hand axis next to delivery performance. Determine the trick.
options: Two scales — the lines appear to move together
questions.why: Are both lines on the same axis? See §5.4.

questions.stem: Select the two polite requests that would settle the supplier's chart.
options: 'Could I see it with the axis from zero and the full period?' and 'Could both lines be on the same axis?'
'Can you lower the price?' and 'Can you sign now?'
'Why so many lines?' and 'Why so few months?'
questions.why: Polite requests, not accusations. See §5.4 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Classify a chart of complaint counts per branch where branches differ wildly in size.
options: Missing base — per customer or per hour would be fair
questions.why: Per what? See §5.4.

questions.stem: Analyse 'on-time delivery rose while complaints fell'. Determine three explanations other than one causing the other.
options: Complaints fell for another reason; a third thing such as season changed both; coincidence over six months
The supplier is honest; the chart is true; the numbers are large
questions.why: Three alternatives to causation. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Classify 'advertising spend and sales rose together, so advertising works'.
options: A correlation that may run the other way — sales released the budget
questions.why: It may run the other way. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Analyse 'ice cream and sunburn rise together'. Determine the third thing.
questions.why: In business the third thing is usually the season, a holiday or a competitor. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Select the evidence that moves a correlation toward a cause.
options: A mechanism, the right sequence, and the problem present here and not there
A bigger sample of the same correlation
questions.why: Mechanism, sequence, IS NOT. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Select the correctly written threshold.
options: 'A fall of more than 15% in average visits counts as yes'
'We will decide after we see the data'
questions.why: Write the threshold as a number, in advance. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a group that collects data first and decides what it means afterwards. Determine the chapter's warning.
options: Any result can be read as supporting what they already believed
It is required for the project
questions.why: Confirmation bias with a spreadsheet. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Determine what to write if you cannot say what result would show your cause is wrong.
options: Your question is not answerable — rewrite it
questions.why: If you cannot, your question is not answerable. See Exercise 4 and §5.6.

questions.stem: Select the best one-sentence question for step 1.
options: 'Are regulars visiting less often than last year?'
questions.why: One sentence, answerable yes or no. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a staff survey of people still employed about why colleagues resign. Determine the flaw.
options: Survivor bias — the ones who left are not in the room
questions.why: Analyse the ones who stayed, conclude about the ones who left. See §5.1.

questions.stem: Determine which numbers to put in a report about queue times of 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 40 minutes.
options: Median 5 and range 3–40, with a note on the single 40
questions.why: Median and range together. See §5.2.

questions.stem: Analyse 'sales rose 200%' for a product that went from 2 units to 6. Determine the honest line.
questions.why: Raw number beside the percentage. See §5.3.

questions.stem: Determine the source line for 'are regulars visiting less?'.
options: The loyalty database, via the marketing manager
questions.why: Where it exists and who can give it. See §5.6.

questions.stem: Analyse the claim 'every number in this chart is accurate, so the chart is honest'. Determine the chapter's reply.
options: Every number can be true while the picture is wrong — check axis, window, scales and base
Accurate numbers make an honest chart
questions.why: True numbers, false picture. See §5.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a one-month rise in both staff overtime and sales. Determine the safest statement.
options: 'They rose together; we do not yet know which, if either, caused the other'
questions.why: Say which of the four you are holding. See §5.5.

questions.stem: Classify 'we will know it worked if things improve' as a threshold.
options: Not a threshold — no number, so any result can be read as success
questions.why: Thresholds are numbers set in advance. See §5.6.
